claim: AutoMitoC is a novel method for array-based mtDNA-CN estimation suitable for biobank-scale studies.
source: We developed a novel method for array-based mtDNA-CN estimation suitable for biobank-scale studies, called 'automatic mitochondrial copy (AutoMitoC).'
evidence: The method is described in the manuscript and validated against other methods.

claim: AutoMitoC was applied to 395,781 UKBiobank study participants.
source: We applied AutoMitoC to 395,781 UKBiobank study participants and performed genome- and exome-wide association studies, identifying novel common and rare genetic determinants.
evidence: Sample size is stated in the abstract and methods.

claim: Genetic analyses identified 71 loci for mtDNA-CN.
source: Overall, genetic analyses identified 71 loci for mtDNA-CN, which implicated several genes involved in rare mtDNA depletion disorders, deoxynucleoside triphosphate (dNTP) metabolism, and the MT central dogma.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the GWAS and ExWAS analyses.

claim: SAMHD1 mutation carriers have higher mtDNA-CN (beta = 0.23 SDs; 95% CI, 0.18–0.29; p=2.6 × 10-19).
source: Rare variant analysis identified SAMHD1 mutation carriers as having higher mtDNA-CN (beta = 0.23 SDs; 95% CI, 0.18–0.29; p=2.6 × 10-19), a potential therapeutic target for patients with mtDNA depletion disorders, but at increased risk of breast cancer (OR = 1.91; 95% CI, 1.52–2.40; p=2.7 × 10-8).
evidence: Statistical association from ExWAS analysis with effect size and p-value.

claim: SAMHD1 mutation carriers have increased risk of breast cancer (OR = 1.91; 95% CI, 1.52–2.40; p=2.7 × 10-8).
source: Rare variant analysis identified SAMHD1 mutation carriers as having higher mtDNA-CN (beta = 0.23 SDs; 95% CI, 0.18–0.29; p=2.6 × 10-19), a potential therapeutic target for patients with mtDNA depletion disorders, but at increased risk of breast cancer (OR = 1.91; 95% CI, 1.52–2.40; p=2.7 × 10-8).
evidence: Statistical association from phenome-wide association testing with odds ratio and p-value.

claim: Low mtDNA-CN has a causal effect on dementia risk (OR = 1.94 per 1 SD decrease in mtDNA-CN; 95% CI, 1.55–2.32; p=7.5 × 10-4).
source: Finally, Mendelian randomization analyses suggest a causal effect of low mtDNA-CN on dementia risk (OR = 1.94 per 1 SD decrease in mtDNA-CN; 95% CI, 1.55–2.32; p=7.5 × 10-4).
evidence: Mendelian randomization analysis provides evidence for causality.

claim: mtDNA-CN is a complex biomarker reflecting specific MT processes related to mtDNA regulation.
source: Altogether, our genetic findings indicate that mtDNA-CN is a complex biomarker reflecting specific MT processes related to mtDNA regulation, and that these processes are causally related to human diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic analyses and pathway enrichment.

claim: MT processes related to mtDNA regulation are causally related to human diseases.
source: Altogether, our genetic findings indicate that mtDNA-CN is a complex biomarker reflecting specific MT processes related to mtDNA regulation, and that these processes are causally related to human diseases.
evidence: This conclusion is based on Mendelian randomization findings.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated as the underlying cause for many human disorders based on mechanistic in vitro and in vivo studies.
source: Mitochondrial (MT) dysfunction has been implicated as the underlying cause for many human disorders based on mechanistic in vitro and in vivo studies (Burbulla et al., 2017; Desdín-Micó et al., 2020; Sliter et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mtDNA-CN is an MT-derived marker that can be conveniently measured from peripheral blood.
source: Complementary evidence comes from recent epidemiological studies that measure mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtDNA-CN), an MT-derived marker that can be conveniently measured from peripheral blood.
evidence: This is a description of the biomarker based on established knowledge.

claim: The ratio of mtDNA to nuclear DNA molecules (mtDNA-CN) in a sample serves as an accessible marker of MT DNA abundance per cell.
source: Since mitochondria contain their own unique set of genomes that are distinct from the nuclear genome, the ratio of mtDNA to nuclear DNA molecules (mtDNA-CN) in a sample serves as an accessible marker of MT DNA abundance per cell (Longchamps et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation.

claim: Individuals with lower mtDNA-CN are at higher risk of age-related complex diseases, such as coronary artery disease, sudden cardiac death, cardiomegaly, stroke, portal hypertension, and chronic kidney disease.
source: Indeed, observational studies suggest that individuals with lower mtDNA-CN are at higher risk of age-related complex diseases, such as coronary artery disease, sudden cardiac death, cardiomegaly, stroke, portal hypertension, and chronic kidney disease (Tin et al., 2016; Ashar et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017; Hägg et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to observational studies.

claim: Higher mtDNA-CN levels have been associated with increased cancer incidence.
source: Conversely, higher mtDNA-CN levels have been associated with increased cancer incidence (Kim et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In cases of mtDNA depletion syndrome, rare defects in nuclear genes responsible for replicating and/or maintaining mtDNA lead to deficient mtDNA-CN.
source: For example, in cases of mtDNA depletion syndrome, wherein rare defects in nuclear genes responsible for replicating and/or maintaining mtDNA lead to deficient mtDNA-CN (Gorman et al., 2016), patients manifest with severe dysfunction of energy-dependent tissues (heart, brain, liver, and cardiac and skeletal muscles).
evidence: This is a description of a known genetic syndrome supported by citation.

claim: Patients with mtDNA depletion syndrome manifest with severe dysfunction of energy-dependent tissues (heart, brain, liver, and cardiac and skeletal muscles).
source: For example, in cases of mtDNA depletion syndrome, wherein rare defects in nuclear genes responsible for replicating and/or maintaining mtDNA lead to deficient mtDNA-CN (Gorman et al., 2016), patients manifest with severe dysfunction of energy-dependent tissues (heart, brain, liver, and cardiac and skeletal muscles).
evidence: This is a clinical description of the syndrome supported by citation.

claim: 19 genes have been reported to cause mtDNA depletion.
source: So far, 19 genes have been reported to cause mtDNA depletion (Oyston, 1998).
evidence: This is a count of known genes supported by citation.

claim: Approximately 50 common loci have been identified for mtDNA-CN regulation.
source: In addition to these rare monogenic syndromes, the importance of common genetic variation in regulating mtDNA-CN is an active area of research with approximately 50 common loci identified so far (Cai et al., 2015; Guyatt et al., 2019; Longchamps, 2019; Hägg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of previous GWAS findings supported by citations.

claim: In rare mtDNA depletion syndromes, mtDNA-CN drops by 60–80%.
source: In contrast to marked drops in mtDNA-CN by 60–80% as seen in those with rare mtDNA depletion syndromes, the relevance of subtler perturbations in mtDNA-CN in disease risk remains to be determined (Basel, 2020).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the syndrome supported by citation.

claim: Many studies show only moderate correlation between mtDNA-CN and markers of MT function or biogenesis.
source: Granted, the connection between blood mtDNA-CN and aspects of MT biology remains unclear with many studies showing only moderate correlation between mtDNA-CN and markers of MT function or biogenesis (Frahm et al., 2005; Wachsmuth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings supported by citations.

claim: Blood mtDNA-CN is strongly confounded by blood cell composition, particularly platelets that are devoid of nuclei.
source: Further complicating the interpretation of epidemiological associations between blood mtDNA-CN and disease risk is the fact that (i) blood mtDNA-CN is strongly confounded by blood cell composition, particularly, platelets that are devoid of nuclei and that (ii) blood mtDNA-CN does not correlate well with mtDNA-CN measured in other tissues in which MT dysfunction may be more relevant (Picard, 2021).
evidence: This is a known confounding factor supported by citation.

claim: Blood mtDNA-CN does not correlate well with mtDNA-CN measured in other tissues in which MT dysfunction may be more relevant.
source: Further complicating the interpretation of epidemiological associations between blood mtDNA-CN and disease risk is the fact that (i) blood mtDNA-CN is strongly confounded by blood cell composition, particularly, platelets that are devoid of nuclei and that (ii) blood mtDNA-CN does not correlate well with mtDNA-CN measured in other tissues in which MT dysfunction may be more relevant (Picard, 2021).
evidence: This is a limitation of blood-based measurements supported by citation.

claim: AutoMitoC replaces autosomal signal normalization of common variants with globally rare variants which negates the need for linkage disequilibrium pruning.
source: First, AutoMitoC replaces autosomal signal normalization of common variants with globally rare variants which negates the need for linkage disequilibrium pruning (Materials and Methods, Figure 1—figure supplements 3–4).
evidence: This is a methodological innovation described in the manuscript.

claim: AutoMitoC empirically assesses the association of corrected probe signal intensities with off-target genome intensities to detect potentially cross-hybridizing probes.
source: Second, to detect potentially cross-hybridizing probes, we empirically assess the association of corrected probe signal intensities with off-target genome intensities (Materials and Methods, Supplementary file 1 – Tab 1–2), rather than relying on sequence homology of probe sequences, which is not always available.
evidence: This is a methodological innovation described in the manuscript.

claim: AutoMitoC ascertains the primary estimate of MT signal using principal component analysis (PCA) as opposed to using the median signal intensity of MT probes.
source: Last, the primary estimate of MT signal is ascertained using principal component analysis ([PCA]; as opposed to using the median signal intensity of MT probes as per the MitoPipeline) which improves concordance of array-based mtDNA-CN estimates with those derived from alternative methods (Materials and Methods).
evidence: This is a methodological innovation that improves performance.

claim: AutoMitoC estimates were significantly correlated with WES estimates (r = 0.45; p<2.23 × 10–308) in 34,436 UKBiobank participants.
source: AutoMitoC estimates were significantly correlated with WES estimates (r = 0.45; p<2.23 × 10–308).
evidence: This is a validation result comparing AutoMitoC to WES-based estimates.

claim: AutoMitoC demonstrated stronger correlation with qPCR-based estimates (r = 0.64; p<2.23 × 10–308) in 5791 participants.
source: Indeed, we observed stronger correlation between AutoMitoC and qPCR-based estimates (r = 0.64; p<2.23 × 10–308; Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a validation result comparing AutoMitoC to qPCR measurements.

claim: AutoMitoC demonstrated robust performance (r > 0.53) across all ethnic strata including Europeans, Latin Americans, Africans, South East Asians, South Asians, and others.
source: Furthermore, AutoMitoC demonstrated robust performance (r > 0.53) across all ethnic strata in the secondary validation cohort including Europeans (N = 2431), Latin Americans (N = 1704), Africans (N = 542), South East Asians (N = 471), South Asians (N = 186), and others (N = 360; ; Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This demonstrates the method's performance across diverse populations.

claim: Every decade increase in age was associated with lower mtDNA-CN levels (beta = −0.08 SDs; 95% CI, –0.07 to –0.08; p<2.23 × 10–308).
source: Consistent with previous reports, every decade increase in age was associated with lower levels (beta = −0.08 SDs; 95% CI, –0.07 to –0.08; p<2.23 × 10–308), and females had higher levels than males (beta = 0.12 SDs; 95% CI, 0.11–0.12; p=1.67 × 10–299).
evidence: This is an association finding consistent with previous reports.

claim: Females had higher mtDNA-CN levels than males (beta = 0.12 SDs; 95% CI, 0.11–0.12; p=1.67 × 10–299).
source: Consistent with previous reports, every decade increase in age was associated with lower levels (beta = −0.08 SDs; 95% CI, –0.07 to –0.08; p<2.23 × 10–308), and females had higher levels than males (beta = 0.12 SDs; 95% CI, 0.11–0.12; p=1.67 × 10–299).
evidence: This is an association finding consistent with previous reports.

claim: South Asians had significantly lower mtDNA-CN levels than Europeans (beta = −0.18; 95% CI, –0.16 to –0.21; p=2.93 × 10–47).
source: MtDNA-CN levels also differed between ethnicities with South Asians (beta = −0.18; 95% CI, –0.16 to –0.21; p=2.93 × 10–47) and Africans (beta = −0.18; 95% CI, –0.16 to –0.21; p=8.39 × 10–48) having significantly lower levels than Europeans.
evidence: This is an association finding showing ethnic differences.

claim: Africans had significantly lower mtDNA-CN levels than Europeans (beta = −0.18; 95% CI, –0.16 to –0.21; p=8.39 × 10–48).
source: MtDNA-CN levels also differed between ethnicities with South Asians (beta = −0.18; 95% CI, –0.16 to –0.21; p=2.93 × 10–47) and Africans (beta = −0.18; 95% CI, –0.16 to –0.21; p=8.39 × 10–48) having significantly lower levels than Europeans.
evidence: This is an association finding showing ethnic differences.

claim: Age, sex, and ethnicity accounted for 0.83% of the phenotypic variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
source: Collectively, age, sex, and ethnicity accounted for 0.83% of the phenotypic variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
evidence: This is a variance explained calculation from regression analysis.

claim: White blood cell count was associated with mtDNA-CN (beta = −0.25 SDs; 95% CI, –0.25 to –0.24; p<2.23–308) and accounted for 6.3% of the variance.
source: All types of cell counts were significantly associated with mtDNA-CN including the standard set of covariates commonly adjusted for in mtDNA-CN investigations, namely, white blood cells (beta = −0.25 SDs in mtDNA-CN levels per 1 SD increase in cell counts; 95% CI, –0.25 to –0.24; p<2.23–308) and platelets (beta = 0.07; 95% CI, 0.06–0.07; p<2.23 × 10–308) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an association finding with variance explained.

claim: Platelet count was associated with mtDNA-CN (beta = 0.07; 95% CI, 0.06–0.07; p<2.23 × 10–308) and accounted for 0.5% of the variance.
source: All types of cell counts were significantly associated with mtDNA-CN including the standard set of covariates commonly adjusted for in mtDNA-CN investigations, namely, white blood cells (beta = −0.25 SDs in mtDNA-CN levels per 1 SD increase in cell counts; 95% CI, –0.25 to –0.24; p<2.23–308) and platelets (beta = 0.07; 95% CI, 0.06–0.07; p<2.23 × 10–308) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an association finding with variance explained.

claim: Neutrophil count (beta = −0.31; 95% CI, –0.31 to –0.30; p<2.23–308) was the strongest predictor of mtDNA-CN levels and accounted for 9.9% of the variance.
source: Notably, neutrophil count (beta = −0.31; 95% CI, –0.31 to –0.30; p<2.23–308) was the strongest predictor of mtDNA-CN levels and accounted for more variance (9.9%) than white blood cell and platelet counts combined (8.2%).
evidence: This is an association finding with variance explained.

claim: Total white blood cell, platelet, and neutrophil counts explained 12.3% variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
source: Collectively, total white blood cell, platelet, and neutrophil counts explained 12.3% variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
evidence: This is a combined variance explained calculation.

claim: A GWAS was performed testing the association of 11,453,766 common genetic variants (MAF >0.005) with mtDNA-CN in 383,476 UKBiobank participants of European ancestry.
source: A GWAS was performed testing the association of 11,453,766 common genetic variants (MAF >0.005) with mtDNA-CN in 383,476 UKBiobank participants of European ancestry (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the GWAS design and sample size.

claim: 9602 variants were associated with mtDNA-CN at genome-wide significance, encompassing 82 independent signals in 72 loci.
source: In total, 9602 variants were associated with mtDNA-CN at genome-wide significance (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), encompassing 82 independent signals in 72 loci (Supplementary file 2 – Tab 1; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary GWAS finding.

claim: The genomic inflation factor was 1.16 and the LD score intercept was 1.036.
source: The genomic inflation factor was 1.16 and the LD score intercept was 1.036, indicating that most inflation in test statistics was attributable to polygenicity.
evidence: These are quality control metrics from the GWAS.

claim: Most inflation in test statistics was attributable to polygenicity.
source: The genomic inflation factor was 1.16 and the LD score intercept was 1.036, indicating that most inflation in test statistics was attributable to polygenicity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the LD score intercept.

claim: NUMT interference may have played a role in two independent signals (two loci), which were subsequently discarded, leading to a total of 80 independent signals in 70 loci.
source: Sensitivity analyses revealed that nuclear mitochondrial DNA (NUMT) interference may have played a role in two independent signals (two loci), which were subsequently discarded, leading to a total of 80 independent signals in 70 loci.
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analyses.

claim: 80 independent genetic signals explained 1.48% variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
source: These 80 independent genetic signals explained 1.48% variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
evidence: This is a variance explained calculation from GWAS.

claim: 17 (22%) of 80 independent genetic associations mapped to a single candidate causal variant.
source: Of the 80 independent genetic associations, 17 (22%) mapped to a single candidate causal variant; 32 (39%) mapped to 5 or fewer variants, and 42 (51%) mapped to 10 or fewer variants (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 2 – Tab 2).
evidence: This is a result from fine-mapping analysis.

claim: Credible sets for 11 genetic signals overlapped with genes responsible for rare mtDNA depletion disorders including DGUOK, MGME1, TFAM, TWNK, POLG2, and TYMP.
source: Credible sets for 11 genetic signals overlapped with genes responsible for rare mtDNA depletion disorders including DGUOK (3), MGME1 (2), TFAM (2), TWNK (2), POLG2 (1), and TYMP (1) (Supplementary file 2 – Tab 1 & 2).
evidence: This is a result from fine-mapping showing overlap with known disease genes.

claim: 10 (53%) of 19 known mtDNA depletion genes harbored at least suggestive mtDNA-CN associations (p<5 × 10–6).
source: Given these observations, we hypothesized that mtDNA depletion genes may be generally enriched for common variant associations. Indeed, 10 (53%) of 19 known mtDNA depletion genes (Oyston, 1998) harbored at least suggestive mtDNA-CN associations (p<5 × 10–6).
evidence: This is an enrichment finding based on hypothesis testing.

claim: Of the 66 independent signals identified by Hägg et al., 2021, 43 (65%) were detected at Bonferroni significance in the present study.
source: Of the 66 independent signals identified by Hägg et al., 2021, we found varying levels of evidence to support 43 (65%) genetic associations; 41 (62%) variants were detected at Bonferroni significance; 2 (3%) variants were detected using a suggestive significance threshold (p<5 × 10–6) (Supplementary file 2 – Tab 3).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous GWAS findings.

claim: 48 (60%) of the 80 genetic associations are likely novel relative to Hägg et al., 2021.
source: While we could not perform the reverse lookup of our top GWAS hits within the Hägg et al., 2021 GWAS due to a lack of full genome-wide summary statistics, 48 (60%) of our 80 genetic associations are likely novel relative to Hägg et al., 2021 as these variants were not reported as genome-wide significant nor in linkage disequilibrium (r2 >0.10) with their top hits (Supplementary file 2 – Tab 1).
evidence: This is a comparison showing novel findings.

claim: Of the 116 detectable variants from Longchamps et al., 2022, 112 (97%) showed varying levels of evidence in the present study.
source: Of the 116 detectable variants, we found varying levels of evidence to support 112 (97%) genetic associations; 70 (60%) variants were detected at Bonferroni significance; 15 (13%) variants were detected using a suggestive significance threshold; 27 (24%) variants were detected at nominal significance with concordant directionality (Supplementary file 2 – Tab 4).
evidence: This is a comparison with another recent GWAS.

claim: 11 (14%) of the 80 genetic associations are likely novel as they were not reported in Hägg et al., 2021 or Longchamps et al., 2022.
source: While we could not perform the reverse lookup of our top GWAS hits within the Longchamps et al., 2022 GWAS, 11 (14%) of our 80 genetic associations are likely novel as these variants were not reported as genome-wide significant nor in linkage disequilibrium with their top hits (Supplementary file 2 – Tab 1). Notably, these 11 associations were also not reported in Hägg et al., 2021.
evidence: This is a comparison showing novel findings.

claim: European effect estimates were significantly and highly correlated with those derived from South Asian (r = 0.97; p=2.2 × 10–15) and African (r = 0.88; p=9.1 × 10–5) GWAS analyses.
source: However, European effect estimates were significantly and highly correlated with those derived from South Asian (r = 0.97; p=2.2 × 10–15) and African (r = 0.88; p=9.1 × 10–5) GWAS analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a transethnic comparison of effect estimates.

claim: Nonsynonymous variants in LONP1 (rs11085147) and TBRG4 (rs2304693), as well as an intronic variant in MRPS35 (rs1127787), were associated with changes in MT gene expression across various tissues.
source: Nonsynonymous variants in LONP1 (rs11085147) and TBRG4 (rs2304693), as well as an intronic variant in MRPS35 (rs1127787), were associated with changes in MT gene expression across various tissues (Supplementary file 2 – Tab 5).
evidence: This is a result from mt-eQTL lookup analysis.

claim: 4 heteroplasmy loci were also associated with mtDNA-CN at genome-wide significance including variants nearby or within TINCR/LONP1, TWNK/MPRL43, TFAM, and PRKAB1 genes.
source: Of 19 matching variants between the GWAS, 4 heteroplasmy loci were also associated with mtDNA-CN at genome-wide significance including variants nearby or within TINCR/LONP1 (rs12461806; mtDNA-CN GWAS p=7.5 × 10–88), TWNK/MPRL43 (rs58678340; p=1.3 × 10–39), TFAM (rs1049432; p=1.5 × 10–21), and PRKAB1 (rs11064881; p=2.6 × 10–10) genes.
evidence: This is a result from heteroplasmy loci lookup.

claim: DEPICT analysis led to the prioritization of 91 out of 18,922 genes (FDR p<0.05).
source: DEPICT analysis led to the prioritization of 91 out of 18,922 genes (false discovery rate (FDR) p<0.05; Supplementary file 2 – Tab 6).
evidence: This is a result from gene prioritization analysis.

claim: GeneMANIA analysis discovered an additional 20 related genes.
source: GeneMANIA analysis discovered an additional 20 related genes (Supplementary file 2 – Tab 7).
evidence: This is a result from network analysis.

claim: Among the 107 total genes prioritized by DEPICT or GeneMANIA, MT functions were significantly enriched in gene ontology terms including mitochondrion organization, MT nucleoid, MT genome maintenance, and MT matrix.
source: Among the 107 total genes prioritized by DEPICT or GeneMANIA (Figure 3C), MT functions were significantly enriched in gene ontology (GO) terms including mitochondrion organization (coverage: 12/225 genes; FDR p=7.4 × 10–5), MT nucleoid (6/34; FDR p=2.2 × 10–4), MT genome maintenance (4/10; FDR p=6.8 × 10–4), and MT matrix (11/257; FDR p=6.8 × 10–4).
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis.

claim: PPRC1 is a potential coordinator of mtDNA-related processes.
source: Visual inspection of the links between key genes involved in these functions highlights PPRC1, a member of the Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma coactivator-1alpha (PGC-1A) family of MT biogenesis activators (Scarpulla, 2011), as a potential coordinator of mtDNA-related processes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference from network analysis and known biology.

claim: 27 (25%) of 107 prioritized genes had evidence of MT localization corresponding to a 4.2-fold enrichment (p=1.0 × 10–10).
source: Overall, 27 (25%) of 107 genes had evidence of MT localization corresponding to a 4.2-fold enrichment (null expectation = 5.9%; p=1.0 × 10–10).
evidence: This is an enrichment analysis result using MitoCarta3.

claim: PGC-1A induction resulted in a higher mean fold change among prioritized genes (beta = 1.48; 95% CI, 0.60–2.37) as compared to any MT gene (beta = 1.19; 95% CI, –0.76–3.13; t-test p=0.04).
source: PGC-1A induction resulted in a higher mean fold change among prioritized genes (beta = 1.48; 95% CI, 0.60–2.37) as compared to any MT gene (beta = 1.19; 95% CI, –0.76–3.13; t-test p=0.04).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of gene expression changes.

claim: Most (16; 57%) of the 27 MitoCarta3 genes were members of the 'Mitochondrial central dogma' pathway, representing a nearly threefold enrichment (p=1.3 × 10–5).
source: Most (16; 57%) genes were members of the 'Mitochondrial central dogma' pathway, which represents a nearly threefold enrichment as compared to the frequency of this pathway in the whole MitoCarta3 database (null expectation = 20.7%; p=1.3 × 10–5).
evidence: This is a pathway enrichment analysis result.

claim: SAMHD1 was the only gene reaching exome-wide significance in the ExWAS.
source: Among 18,890 genes tested, SAMHD1 was the only gene reaching exome-wide significance (Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is the primary finding from ExWAS analysis.

claim: The carrier prevalence of rare SAMHD1 mutations was 0.75%.
source: The carrier prevalence of rare SAMHD1 mutations was 0.75%, and on average, mutation carriers had higher mtDNA-CN than noncarriers (beta = 0.23 SDs; 95% CI, 0.18–0.29; p=2.6 × 10–19; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the ExWAS.

claim: A suggestive association was found for TFAM (beta = −0.33; 95% CI, –0.47 to –0.19; p=4.2 × 10–6) in the ExWAS.
source: Also, while none of the 19 known mtDNA depletion genes reached Bonferroni significance, a suggestive association was found for TFAM (beta = −0.33; 95% CI, –0.47 to –0.19; p=4.2 × 10–6), and this association was independent of the common TFAM variants (rs12247015; rs4397793) previously identified in the GWAS (beta = −0.33; 95% CI, –0.47 to –0.19; p=8 × 10–6).
evidence: This is a finding from ExWAS analysis.

claim: Rare variants in SAMHD1 and TFAM accounted for 0.06% of the variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
source: Rare variants in SAMHD1 and TFAM accounted for 0.06% of the variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
evidence: This is a variance explained calculation from ExWAS.

claim: Rare and common loci collectively accounted for 1.55% of variance in mtDNA-CN levels.
source: Collectively, rare and common loci accounted for 1.55%.
evidence: This is a combined variance explained calculation.

claim: SAMHD1 mutation carrier status was associated with approximately twofold increased risk of breast cancer (OR = 1.91; 95% CI, 1.52–2.40; p=2.7 × 10–8).
source: At phenome-wide significance, SAMHD1 mutation carrier status was associated with approximately twofold increased risk of breast cancer (OR = 1.91; 95% CI, 1.52–2.40; p=2.7 × 10–8), as well as greater risk of 'cancer (suspected or other)' (OR = 1.52; 95% CI, 1.28–1.80; p=1.1 × 10–6; Figure 4B; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from phenome-wide association testing.

claim: SAMHD1 mutation carrier status was associated with greater risk of 'cancer (suspected or other)' (OR = 1.52; 95% CI, 1.28–1.80; p=1.1 × 10–6).
source: At phenome-wide significance, SAMHD1 mutation carrier status was associated with approximately twofold increased risk of breast cancer (OR = 1.91; 95% CI, 1.52–2.40; p=2.7 × 10–8), as well as greater risk of 'cancer (suspected or other)' (OR = 1.52; 95% CI, 1.28–1.80; p=1.1 × 10–6; Figure 4B; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from phenome-wide association testing.

claim: The effect of rare SAMHD1 variants on mtDNA-CN levels is not driven by its relationship with cancer status.
source: To understand whether differences in mtDNA-CN levels between SAMHD1 mutation carriers was a consequence of cancer diagnosis, we repeated association testing with mtDNA-CN excluding cancer patients. In this analysis, the association with mtDNA-CN levels was not attenuated (beta = 0.26; 95% CI, 0.19–0.32; p=7.8 × 10–15) suggesting that the effect of rare SAMHD1 variants on mtDNA-CN levels is not driven by its relationship with cancer status.
evidence: This is a conclusion from sensitivity analysis.

claim: After accounting for multiple testing of 10 phenotypes, an association between mtDNA-CN and all-cause dementia was found (OR = 1.94 per 1 SD decrease in mtDNA-CN; 95% CI, 1.55–2.32; p=7.5 × 10–4).
source: After accounting for multiple testing of 10 phenotypes, an association between mtDNA-CN and all-cause dementia was found (OR = 1.94 per 1 SD decrease in mtDNA-CN; 95% CI, 1.55–2.32; p=7.5 × 10–4; Figure 6; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is the primary finding from Mendelian randomization analysis.

claim: Sensitivity analyses indicated no evidence of global (MR-PRESSO p=0.51; Q-statistic p=0.51) or directional (Egger Intercept p=0.47) pleiotropy for the dementia association.
source: Sensitivity analyses indicated no evidence of global (MR-PRESSO p=0.51; Q-statistic p=0.51) or directional (Egger Intercept p=0.47) pleiotropy.
evidence: These are results from MR sensitivity analyses.

claim: The 27 selected variants accounted for 0.70% of the variance in mtDNA-CN and 0.13% of the risk for dementia, consistent with a causal effect of mtDNA-CN on dementia risk and not vice versa (Steiger p=1.9 × 10–62).
source: The 27 selected variants accounted for 0.70% of the variance in mtDNA-CN and 0.13% of the risk for dementia, consistent with a causal effect of mtDNA-CN on dementia risk and not vice versa (Steiger p=1.9 × 10–62).
evidence: This is a result from Steiger directionality test supporting causality.

claim: The dementia association was replicated using a second UKBiobank-independent GWAS dataset from the International Genomics of Alzheimer's Disease Consortium including 17,008 Alzheimer's disease patients (OR = 1.41; 95% CI, 1.0001–1.98; p=0.04993).
source: Furthermore, we replicated the dementia association using a second UKBiobank-independent GWAS dataset derived from the International Genomics of Alzheimer's Disease Consortium (2013) including 17,008 Alzheimer's disease patients (OR = 1.41; 95% CI, 1.0001–1.98; p=0.04993) (Lambert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a replication of the MR finding in an independent dataset.

claim: The present study represents the most comprehensive genetic assessment of mtDNA-CN published to date.
source: While several investigations for mtDNA-CN have been published, the present study represents the most comprehensive genetic assessment published to date (Cai et al., 2015; Longchamps, 2019; Hägg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a claim about the scope of the study relative to previous work.

claim: Hägg et al., 2021 conducted the largest GWAS for mtDNA-CN in 295,150 UKBiobank participants and identified 50 common loci.
source: Notably, Hägg et al., 2021 recently conducted the largest GWAS for mtDNA-CN in 295,150 UKBiobank participants and identified 50 common loci (Hägg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of previous work supported by citation.

claim: AutoMitoC exhibits superior concordance with WES-based estimates (AutoMitoC r = 0.45) compared to Hägg et al., 2021 method (Hagg r = 0.33).
source: In addition, AutoMitoC exhibits superior concordance with WES-based estimates (Hagg r = 0.33; AutoMitoC r = 0.45), which were validated in an independent dataset with gold standard qPCR measurements (AutoMitoC r = 0.64).
evidence: This is a comparison of method performance.

claim: Differences in mtDNA-CN reflect MT processes related to dNTP metabolism and the replication, maintenance, and organization of mtDNA.
source: Primarily, differences in mtDNA-CN reflect MT processes related to dNTP metabolism and the replication, maintenance, and organization of mtDNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion from pathway enrichment analyses.

claim: The observed enrichment in common variant associations within mtDNA depletion genes reinforces the notion that differences in mtDNA-CN first and foremost reflect perturbations in mtDNA-related processes.
source: The observed enrichment in common variant associations within mtDNA depletion genes further reinforces the notion that differences in mtDNA-CN first and foremost reflect perturbations in mtDNA-related processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the enrichment findings.

claim: SAMHD1 is a multifaceted enzyme with various functions including tumor suppression through DNA repair activity and maintenance of steady-state intracellular dNTP levels.
source: SAMHD1 is a multifaceted enzyme with various functions including tumor suppression through DNA repair activity and maintenance of steady-state intracellular dNTP levels, which has been involved in HIV-1 replication (Baldauf et al., 2012; Kretschmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of SAMHD1 function supported by citations.

claim: Rare homozygous and compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in SAMHD1 result in Aicardi Goutieres' syndrome.
source: Rare homozygous and compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in SAMHD1 result in an immune encephalopathy known as Aicardi Goutieres' syndrome (White et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of a genetic syndrome supported by citation.

claim: In the UKBiobank, the vast majority (99.4%) of individuals possessing SAMHD1 mutations were heterozygote carriers.
source: In the UKBiobank, the vast majority (99.4%) of individuals possessing SAMHD1 mutations were heterozygote carriers, who had a twofold increased risk of breast cancer.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study data.

claim: Higher mtDNA-CN is not always a protective signature of proper MT function and healthy cells.
source: Indeed, our finding that SAMHD1 mutations associate with both elevated mtDNA-CN levels and risk of breast cancer belies the prevailing notion that higher mtDNA-CN is always a protective signature of proper MT function and healthy cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation challenging a prevailing assumption.

claim: Approximately 1 in 130 UKBiobank participants possessed a SAMHD1 genetic mutation conferring twofold elevated risk of breast cancer.
source: First, heterozygous SAMHD1 mutations may be an overlooked risk factor for breast cancer considering that ~1 in 130 UKBiobank participants possessed a genetic mutation conferring twofold elevated risk.
evidence: This is calculated from the carrier prevalence of 0.75% (approximately 1/133).

claim: SAMHD1 is not routinely screened nor part of targeted gene panels outside the context of neurological disorders.
source: Notably, while SAMHD1 mutations have been described previously to be associated with various cancers (Kohnken et al., 2015; Rentoft, 2019), this gene is not routinely screened nor part of targeted gene panels outside the context of neurological disorders (https://www.genedx.com/test-catalog/available-tests/comprehensive-common-cancer-panel/).
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice supported by citation and reference to a clinical resource.

claim: Therapeutic strategies to dampen (but not abolish) SAMHD1 activity might be considered to treat mtDNA depletion disorders caused by defects in nucleotide metabolism.
source: Third, while SAMHD1 is a highly pleiotropic protein, therapeutic strategies to dampen (but not abolish) SAMHD1 activity might be considered to treat mtDNA depletion disorders caused by defects in nucleotide metabolism.
evidence: This is a therapeutic speculation based on the findings.

claim: Franzolin et al., 2015 demonstrated that siRNA knockdown of SAMHD1 in human fibroblasts with DGUOK mtDNA depletion mutations partially recovered mtDNA-CN.
source: Indeed, Franzolin et al., 2015 demonstrated that siRNA knockdown of SAMHD1 in human fibroblasts with DGUOK mtDNA depletion mutations partially recovered mtDNA-CN (Franzolin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of previous experimental work supported by citation.

claim: This study provides the first Mendelian randomization evidence that mtDNA-CN may be causally related to risk of dementia.
source: To our knowledge, we provide the first Mendelian randomization evidence that mtDNA-CN may be causally related to risk of dementia.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Silzer et al., 2019 showed that individuals with cognitive impairment had significantly lower blood-based mtDNA-CN in a matched case-control study of 46 participants.
source: Silzer et al., 2019 conducted a matched case-control study of 46 participants and showed that individuals with cognitive impairment had significantly lower blood-based mtDNA-CN (Silzer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of previous work supported by citation.

claim: Andrews and Goate, 2020 found that a 1 SD decrease in brain mtDNA-CN was associated with lower mini mental state exam (beta = –4.02; 95% CI, –5.49 to –2.55; p=1.07 × 10–7) and higher clinical dementia rating (beta = 0.71; 95% CI, 0.51–0.91) in 1025 postmortem brain tissue samples.
source: Andrews and Goate, 2020 studied the relationship between postmortem brain tissue mtDNA-CN and measures of cognitive impairment in 1025 samples (Andrews and Goate, 2020). Consistent with our findings, a 1 SD decrease in brain mtDNA-CN was associated with lower mini mental state exam (beta = –4.02; 95% CI, –5.49 to –2.55; p=1.07 × 10–7) and higher clinical dementia rating (beta = 0.71; 95% CI, 0.51–0.91).
evidence: This is a description of previous work supported by citation.

claim: Yang et al., 2021 observed a significant association between mtDNA-CN and incident risk of neurodegenerative disease (Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease).
source: In contrast, Yang et al., 2021 observed a significant association between mtDNA-CN and incident risk of neurodegenerative disease (Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease)(Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of previous work supported by citation.

claim: mtDNA-CN represents both a marker and mediator of dementia.
source: Altogether, our results combined with previous findings suggest that mtDNA-CN represents both a marker and mediator of dementia.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating current and previous findings.

claim: AutoMitoC was benchmarked using multiple comparative mtDNA-CN estimation modalities, in independent cohorts, and in various ethnic groups.
source: AutoMitoC was benchmarked using multiple comparative mtDNA-CN estimation modalities, in independent cohorts, and in various ethnic groups, but further work can be done to assess the reproducibility and error of mtDNA-CN estimates, calibration to absolute counts, and the robustness to different genotyping platforms.
evidence: This describes the validation approach taken in the study.

claim: Whole genome sequencing will eventually supplant array-based mtDNA-CN GWAS.
source: Although whole genome sequencing will eventually supplant array-based mtDNA-CN GWAS, we hypothesize that the improvements made in the areas of speed, portability to ethnically diverse studies, and ease-of-implementation, should greatly increase accessibility of mtDNA-CN research as a plethora of genotyping array data is presently available to reanalyze.
evidence: This is a speculation about future trends in the field.

claim: Genetic findings indicate that mtDNA-CN is a complex biomarker under substantial nuclear genetic regulation.
source: Although commonly viewed as a simple surrogate marker for the number of mitochondria present within a sample, genetic analyses suggest that mtDNA-CN is a highly complex biomarker under substantial nuclear genetic regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the genetic analyses.

claim: mtDNA-CN reflects a mixture of MT processes mostly pertaining to mtDNA regulation.
source: mtDNA-CN reflects a mixture of MT processes mostly pertaining to mtDNA regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from pathway enrichment analyses.

claim: There is evidence for mtDNA-CN as a putative causal risk factor for dementia.
source: Accordingly, the true relationship between mtDNA-CN measured in blood samples with human disease remains to be completely defined though we find evidence for mtDNA-CN as a putative causal risk factor for dementia.
evidence: This is a conclusion from Mendelian randomization analysis.
